scenes.title: Lumen Eats Launches In A City

visual_beats.directive: City map draws with office blocks
Empty order tickets float outward
Two data stream icons appear

narration.text: Lumen Eats is a city food delivery startup about to launch lunchtime meals. One big risk: nobody wants them. Market research is the process of gathering, analysing and interpreting information about a market. On the map, empty order tickets float over office blocks. The team can ask customers directly, or read data someone else collected. This video follows two information streams, then builds a sample grid, and finally runs a survey with real numbers. Choose well, and a costly launch becomes a calculated one.

visual_beats.directive: Blue stream fills with fieldwork sources
Green stream fills with desk sources
Both streams reach the decision node

narration.text: Two streams appear. Primary market research is the collection and collation of original data via direct contact with potential or existing consumers, also called field research. Questionnaires, interviews, focus groups and observation feed it. Secondary market research uses information that has already been collected and is available for use by others, also called desk research. Competitor websites, government sources, market reports and trade magazines feed that one. One stream is fresh and specific; the other is quick and cheap.

visual_beats.directive: Clock icons tick at different speeds
Price tags drop into each column
Freshness meters settle

narration.text: Fieldwork goes to the customer. Desk research stays at the screen. Fieldwork gives current, specific answers, but it costs time and money, and a poor sample can bias it. Desk research is faster and cheaper, yet data may be outdated or not specific to this city. Lumen Eats puts a clock beside each stream: days for fieldwork, minutes for desk work. A price tag appears beside each: thousands for surveys, almost nothing for a report. The right mix matters more than any single method.

visual_beats.directive: Tick marks fill the questionnaire grid
Focus group bubbles expand
Loaded and neutral questions compare side by side

narration.text: A questionnaire is a set of questions to be answered as a means of collecting data for primary market research. Ticks fill a grid as answers land. Interviews and focus groups go deeper: a group of people representative of the target market discusses opinions about products and promotions. Watch the wording trap. A leading question, Don't you love our menu, pushes people to agree. A neutral question, How often would you order lunch, gives cleaner data. Bad wording distorts every chart that follows.

visual_beats.directive: Population grid of 100 cells draws in
Random cells light in scattered positions
Quota cells light evenly by age band

narration.text: A sample is a group of people selected to respond to a primary market research exercise, such as a questionnaire. Here is a grid of one hundred city workers. First, random sampling: every cell has an equal chance, and twenty cells light up in scattered positions. Next, quota sampling: the grid sorts into age bands, and the researcher picks ten from each band, so the mix matches the target market. Random selection spreads chance; quota selection controls the mix. Both beat asking only friends.

visual_beats.directive: One corner of the grid lights up
Estimate bar jumps too high
Four accuracy dials appear

narration.text: Sample bias is the pitfall. Lumen Eats surveys thirty people outside one gym, and the grid glows in one corner only. Because that sample came from one place, therefore it over represented fitness fans, so the lunch estimate looked far too high. Accuracy depends on sample size, sample bias, question wording, timing and the age of the data. A larger, more representative sample improves reliability. A biased one makes results misleading, however polished the chart looks.

visual_beats.directive: Bars build for 240, 96 and 64
Loaded wording bar jumps to 78 percent
Cost cards compare survey and report

narration.text: Here is the full survey. The target population is eight thousand office workers. A random sample of four hundred replies. Two hundred and forty say they would order lunch, which is sixty percent. Ninety six prefer dinner, and sixty four are unsure. A quota check keeps the age mix even. The same question with loaded wording lifts support to seventy eight percent, a clear warning sign. A desk report costs two hundred dollars but is two years old; the survey costs one thousand two hundred and is current. Recommendation: trust the neutral survey.

scenes.title: Two Streams, One Decision
labels: Primary: specific but costly and biased
Secondary: cheap but generic and old

visual_beats.directive: Six stage timeline clicks into place
Scale compares primary and secondary
Verdict banner highlights neutral survey

narration.text: The stages are clear: set the objective, choose the method, draw the sample, collect, analyse, then recommend. On the split screen, primary data is specific and current, yet costly and prone to bias. Secondary data is quick and cheap, yet generic and possibly outdated. Because this decision is about a local launch, therefore Lumen Eats pays for a neutral survey, so the recommendation rests on fresh evidence. The best research often blends both streams, with a checked sample and careful wording.

recap_quiz.question: A leading question gives 78 percent support; a neutral quota sample gives 60 percent. Which figure should guide Lumen Eats launch?
options: 60 percent, from neutral and even groups
recap_quiz.visual_explanation: Two bars compare the loaded and neutral results while a population grid highlights the even age mix.
